disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c of 7.8% is in the diabetes range, which means your body is having more difficulty managing blood sugar than is typical. Along with this, your BMI of 28.3 falls in the obese range, you have high blood pressure, and your activity level is currently low, all of which add extra strain on your heart, kidneys, and blood vessels. The most valuable next steps are getting your kidney function, vitamin B12, eye, blood pressure, and cardiovascular risk checked soon, building in regular moderate activity, and following the sodium-conscious, DASH-style eating pattern suggested for you. These changes, done consistently, can help you feel more in control of your health over time.

risk_factors.label: Existing health condition: High blood pressure

comorbidity_assessment.note: High blood pressure and elevated blood sugar often affect the same blood vessels and organs, so managing sodium intake and staying active can support both your blood pressure and your blood sugar goals.

constraints: Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day (about one teaspoon of salt in total); avoid pickles, papad, instant noodles and salty snacks.
Follow a DASH-style pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses and low-fat dairy (or fortified alternatives).

foods_to_eat: Whole grains like brown rice, millets (bajra, jowar, ragi) and whole wheat
Pulses and lentils such as moong, masoor and rajma
Fresh vegetables, especially leafy greens, gourds and beans
Fresh fruit like guava, apple, papaya and berries in moderate portions
Low-fat dairy or fortified plant-based alternatives
Nuts and seeds in small handfuls, like almonds or flaxseeds
Herbs and spices such as turmeric, cumin, coriander and mint for flavour instead of salt
foods_to_avoid: Pickles, papad and other high-sodium condiments
Instant noodles and packaged salty snacks
Sugary drinks, sweets and desserts made with refined sugar
Refined flour (maida) products like white bread and biscuits
Deep-fried foods such as samosas, pakoras and puris
Processed and canned foods with added salt
Full-fat dairy products and excess ghee or butter
plan.portion_guidance: Use small bowls (katori) and cups to manage portions within your 1,200 kcal target. Fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with whole grains or millets, and a quarter with pulses, paneer or low-fat dairy. Avoid second helpings and eat slowly to help with fullness.
plan.hydration: Aim for about 8 to 10 glasses of water a day. Herbal teas and plain buttermilk can also help you stay hydrated. Limit sugary beverages and salty packaged drinks.
based_on: high blood pressure: low sodium, DASH-style pattern
HbA1c in the diabetes range: low-glycaemic, high-fibre focus
BMI in obese category: portion-controlled, nutrient-dense meals

exercise: Start with 10-15 minutes of gentle walking or seated exercises most days, as you are currently sedentary.
Gradually build up over several weeks toward at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, which also helps lower blood pressure.
Add simple muscle-strengthening activities, like resistance band exercises or bodyweight moves, on 2 days a week.
Check with your doctor before starting a new exercise routine, especially given your blood pressure, to make sure your plan is safe for you.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with a 10-minute walk, 5 days a week, and build up gradually by adding a few minutes every week until you reach 30 minutes a day, most days of the week.
lifestyle.weight_management: Since your BMI is in the obese range, gradually working toward a healthier weight can help improve your HbA1c and blood pressure over time. Focus on steady, sustainable changes such as portion control, more vegetables and whole grains, and regular activity rather than quick fixes.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, avoid screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet to support restful sleep.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5-10 minutes a day to help calm your body and support healthy blood pressure.
Try gentle yoga or meditation, which are well suited to an Indian lifestyle and can help reduce stress.
Consider setting aside quiet time each day for relaxation or a hobby you enjoy.
behaviour_change: Build physical activity into daily routines, such as short walks after meals, to support both blood sugar and blood pressure.
Track your progress with small, achievable goals to stay motivated and build confidence over time.
Since you don't smoke or drink, keep up these healthy habits as part of your overall plan.

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

preventive_actions: Schedule the highlighted monitoring tests, especially kidney function, vitamin B12, and a dilated eye exam, in the near future.
Aim to keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day by avoiding pickles, papad, instant noodles, and salty snacks.
Build in regular moderate aerobic activity, such as daily walks, to help support both blood sugar and blood pressure.
Follow a DASH-style eating pattern with plenty of vegetables, fruit, pulses, and low-fat dairy or fortified alternatives.
Track your home blood pressure readings so you and your doctor can watch trends over time.
Keep your calorie intake near the suggested 1,200 calorie target to support gradual, steady progress with your weight.
